scope_plain: Every California voter. California uses a top-two system: the two highest vote-getters from the June primary advance regardless of party, so some November races have two candidates from the same party.
office_explainer: Runs the state. Signs or vetoes laws, writes the budget, appoints judges, leads emergency response.
why_it_matters: Gov. Newsom is termed out, so this is an open seat. The next governor controls a roughly $300 billion budget and sets policy on housing, insurance, energy costs and how California deals with the federal government.

candidates.name: Xavier Becerra
candidates.background: Former U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services (2021-2025), California Attorney General (2017-2021), and a member of Congress from Los Angeles for more than two decades. Ballot designation: Voting Rights Attorney.

own_words.text: Health care is a human right
On housing: "treat housing like the essential infrastructure it is." Says he would declare a housing state of emergency on day one to fund 40,000 approved affordable units.
On homelessness: "We have spent billions, and the results are not good enough." Proposes an ongoing state funding stream for rental assistance and a public dashboard tracking state-funded units.
Opposes Proposition 40 (the billionaire wealth tax); supports a progressive income tax; says he would declare an emergency to freeze utility and insurance rates.

candidates.name: Steve Hilton
candidates.background: Former senior adviser to UK Prime Minister David Cameron (2010-2012), co-founder of a Silicon Valley political crowdfunding company, author, and host of a weekly Fox News show from 2017 to 2023. Ballot designation: Small Business Owner.

own_words.text: "First $150,000 Tax Free." Would eliminate state income tax on the first $150,000 of earnings with a flat rate above that.
"$3.00 Gas." Would end state fuel rules and fees he says drove up prices, including halving the gas tax and dropping the Low Carbon Fuel Standard.
"Starter Homes for Young Families." Would cut fees and building rules on smaller single-family homes and limit CEQA lawsuits against construction.
"Every Student Reads by 3rd Grade." Supports phonics instruction and holding back third graders who are not reading at grade level; supports school choice.

scope_plain: Every California voter. Top-two system: both finalists advanced from the June primary.
office_explainer: Fills in for the governor, breaks Senate ties, sits on UC and CSU boards and the State Lands Commission.
why_it_matters: Mostly a standby job, but the holder becomes governor if the office opens up and votes on university tuition and coastal land decisions.
incumbent: Eleni Kounalakis (termed out, running for Treasurer)

candidates.name: Fiona Ma
candidates.background: State Treasurer since 2019. Previously on the Board of Equalization (2014-2018), the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, and four terms in the state Assembly. Certified Public Accountant. Ballot designation: State Treasurer/CPA.

own_words.text: "Too many are being priced out of the California Dream." Says red tape delays housing and discourages investment.
"I will make higher education more affordable, expand paid internships, and strengthen career pathways."
Points to her Treasurer record: financed a record number of affordable housing units and expanded down-payment help for first-time buyers.

candidates.name: Gloria Romero
candidates.background: Former Democratic state senator (about 12 years) and the first woman to serve as Senate Majority Leader (2005-2008). Registered as a Republican in 2024. Republican governor candidate Steve Hilton asked her to run alongside him. Ballot designation: Educator/Businesswoman.

own_words.text: "This office should not be a ceremonial title or a parking spot for failed career politicians."
"I will restore education standards, develop a bold economic plan that helps businesses thrive."
Says she would rein in state commissions on water and farmland, "defend Title IX for our daughters in sports," and fight antisemitism on campuses.

scope_plain: Every California voter. Top-two system: both finalists advanced from the June primary.
office_explainer: Runs statewide elections, certifies results, keeps business filings and campaign finance records.
why_it_matters: This is the state's chief elections officer. The winner oversees how ballots are mailed, counted and audited, and handles voter rolls and election security.

candidates.name: Shirley N. Weber
candidates.background: Secretary of State since 2021 (appointed, then elected to a full term in 2022). Previously served eight years in the state Assembly. Ballot designation: California Secretary of State.

own_words.text: "I will never give up on protecting your voting rights."
"I will continue to fight to make sure that nothing stands between you and the ballot box."
Second-term priorities, per CalMatters: expanding voting access, more transparent election filings, stronger cybersecurity.

candidates.name: Donald P. (Don) Wagner
candidates.background: Orange County Supervisor. Former mayor of Irvine and former state Assemblymember. Ballot designation: Orange County Supervisor.

own_words.text: "I pledge to speed up vote counting, secure our elections, and remove the chief elections officer from partisan politics."
Supports requiring photo ID at the polls: "Thirty-six states and most democratic nations require photo ID at the polls. California does not."
"I will be an umpire for fair elections, not a partisan player."

scope_plain: Every California voter. Top-two system: both finalists advanced from the June primary.
office_explainer: The state's accountant. Audits spending, runs payroll, pays the bills, sits on about 70 boards.
why_it_matters: The controller is the main independent check on how state and local governments spend state money, and holds the fifth seat on the Board of Equalization.

candidates.name: Malia M. Cohen
candidates.background: State Controller since 2023. Former chair of the Board of Equalization and former San Francisco supervisor. Ballot designation: State Controller/Mother.

own_words.text: Running "to ensure taxpayer dollars are managed with transparency, accountability, and fairness."
"budgets are moral documents that should reflect our shared values and invest in people, not special interests."
Points to expanded public access to financial and payroll data, monthly cash reports, and modernizing the state payroll system.

candidates.name: Herb W Morgan
candidates.background: Chief investment officer. Founded a San Diego investment firm later acquired by Cantor Fitzgerald Investment Advisors; worked on San Diego's pension system under Mayor Jerry Sanders. Ballot designation: Chief Investment Officer.

own_words.text: "The State Controller does not set policy." Describes the job as pre-audits, approval of spending, and rigorous post-audits.
Would put "all expenditures in an easy-to-use online database with transaction-level detail and near real-time reporting."
Per the Sacramento Bee, wants to update the state's Fi$Cal accounting system to work in real time and use AI to flag spending problems.

scope_plain: Every California voter. Top-two system: both finalists advanced from the June primary.
office_explainer: The state's banker. Invests public money, sells state bonds, manages debt.
why_it_matters: Open seat. The treasurer decides where billions in idle state cash is invested and runs the bond sales that pay for schools, housing and infrastructure.
incumbent: Fiona Ma (termed out, running for Lt. Governor)

candidates.name: Eleni Kounalakis
candidates.background: Lieutenant Governor since 2019 (two terms). Former U.S. Ambassador to Hungary. Spent nearly two decades as a housing developer before entering politics. Ballot designation: Lieutenant Governor of California.

own_words.text: "I will build more affordable housing through public finance; invest in the financial future of children and families."
Says she would "defend health care and immigrant communities, and protect pensions for hard-working Californians."
Points to votes against tuition increases on the UC Regents and CSU Trustees boards and to 60,000 new college housing beds.

candidates.name: Jennifer Hawks
candidates.background: Retired Silicon Valley business executive with no prior elected office; most recently on the executive team at Sacred Heart Schools in Atherton. Local Republican Party activist. Ballot designation: Retired Business Executive.

own_words.text: "I'm not a career politician. I'm a business professional who has spent my career managing budgets, improving operations, and demanding accountability."
"California needs a financial watchdog, not another politician."
Says the Treasurer cannot rewrite the budget but can "demand transparency, strengthen oversight, and shine a light on how taxpayer dollars are managed."

why_it_matters: The AG decides which lawsuits California files (including against the federal government), writes ballot measure titles, and investigates police shootings.

candidates.name: Rob Bonta
candidates.background: Attorney General since 2021 (appointed, then elected in 2022). Former state Assemblymember from the East Bay. Has filed or joined more than 50 lawsuits against the Trump administration since 2025. Ballot designation: California Attorney General. Did not submit a Voter Information Guide statement.

own_words.text: "protect our freedoms, defend our democracy, and stand up to abuse of power wherever it appears"
"keep our communities safe from gun violence and fentanyl trafficking"
"hold greedy corporations accountable" and "safeguard our environment"

candidates.name: Michael E. Gates
candidates.background: Huntington Beach City Attorney for about a decade; served in 2025 as a deputy assistant attorney general in the U.S. Justice Department Civil Rights Division. Ballot designation: Deputy United States Attorney.

own_words.text: "Californians voted for Prop. 36 overwhelmingly to restore accountability for repeat theft and drug offenses. I will fully enforce it."
"Fentanyl is taking our kids. Retail theft is closing the stores we count on."
"Public safety is not a partisan issue, and I will never treat it like one."

scope_plain: Every California voter. Top-two system: both finalists are Democrats. This is the first time two candidates from the same party have met in a November race for this office.
office_explainer: Regulates insurance companies: approves rates, licenses insurers, handles consumer complaints.
why_it_matters: Open seat in the middle of a home insurance crisis. Insurers have pulled back after wildfires and the FAIR Plan (last-resort insurer) has grown. The commissioner shapes whether and at what price people can get coverage.

candidates.name: Ben Allen
candidates.background: State Senator since 2014 representing the Santa Monica area. Authored the 2024 climate bond (Prop 4) and laws on plastics. Represented districts hit by the 2025 LA fires. Ballot designation: California State Senator.

own_words.text: "I'm not taking any insurance company money because my loyalty is to you."
"I'll increase competition to bring down costs, protect consumers who are unfairly dropped, make insurers accountable."
Prefers "a proven, practical path that adds insurance options and lowers rates" over an "untested large-scale system" that puts the state on the hook.

candidates.name: Jane Kim
candidates.background: Civil rights attorney and former San Francisco Supervisor. Helped pass free community college and a $15 minimum wage in San Francisco. Ballot designation: Attorney/Consumer Advocate.

own_words.text: "California deserves a watchdog for consumers, not a lapdog for corporations."
"I'll make claims fast and fair, cap excessive profits, and crack down on illegal price-fixing."
Proposes a state-run "public Disaster Insurance for All program" funded by premiums, and supports expanding low-cost auto insurance to more drivers.

scope_plain: Every California voter. Nonpartisan office: no party labels on the ballot. It's on the November ballot because no one won a majority in the June primary (Shaw led with about 25%, Barrera had about 20%).
office_explainer: Runs the state Department of Education and speaks for K-12 schools. Nonpartisan.
why_it_matters: About 6 million public school students. Note: starting in 2027, a new law moves much of the department's day-to-day authority to a governor-appointed education commissioner, so the job is changing.

candidates.name: Richard Barrera
candidates.background: President of the San Diego Unified school board, where he has served 18 years. Registered Democrat (the office is nonpartisan). Ballot designation: State Superintendent Advisor.

own_words.text: "I am proud of what our students have achieved in San Diego and look forward to improving student success across California."
Says he will "work with the same energy and zeal to bring those reforms to every school in California," citing San Diego Unified's reading and math gains.
Priorities per CalMatters: school funding, early childhood education, and easing the path to becoming a teacher. Says he will keep ICE out of schools.

candidates.name: Sonja Shaw
candidates.background: President of the Chino Valley Unified school board. Registered Republican (the office is nonpartisan). Ballot designation: School District President.

own_words.text: "My plan is simple: restore high academic standards in reading, writing, and math; protect Title IX, ensuring fairness and safety for girls."
"cut wasteful bureaucracy; and demand fiscal transparency to ensure money reaches classrooms where it belongs"
Says she will "protect the office's independence as voters intended" and stand up to "politicians and special interests."

candidates.name: Nelson Esparza
candidates.background: Fresno City Council member since 2019 and current council president; chairs its Finance and Audit Committee. Economics instructor. Ballot designation: Teacher/Economist/Councilmember.

own_words.text: Will "fight to close tax loopholes and crack down on tax evaders" so local governments can fund public safety, schools and health care.
"Nelson will oppose new taxes on middle class and working class families as well as small businesses."
Wants "more transparency in our tax system" and "fair impartial property tax assessments."

candidates.name: Shannon Grove
candidates.background: State Senator from Bakersfield since 2018, previously in the Assembly. Army veteran. Founded a staffing company. Ballot designation: State Senator/Businesswoman.

Will "make sure the government doesn't overtax your home, your business, or your property."

candidates.background: State Assemblymember since 2014; chairs the Assembly Revenue and Taxation Committee. Former chief of staff to a BOE chairman, former Carson councilmember and police officer. Ballot designation: State Assemblymember/Father.

office: Associate Justice, Supreme Court of California
scope_plain: Every California voter. The ballot asks: "Shall Associate Justice of the Supreme Court Kelli M. Evans be elected to the office for the term provided by law?" Vote YES to keep her or no to remove her. No one runs against her.
office_explainer: One of seven justices on the state's highest court. The final word on California law.
why_it_matters: A majority yes vote keeps the justice. If voters reject the justice, the governor fills the vacancy. In 1986, voters rejected Chief Justice Rose Bird and Justices Cruz Reynoso and Joseph Grodin in retention elections.

candidates.name: Kelli M. Evans
candidates.background: Associate Justice since 2023, appointed by Gov. Newsom. Previously an Alameda County Superior Court judge, chief deputy legal affairs secretary to Gov. Newsom, special assistant attorney general, and an ACLU of Northern California attorney. UC Davis Law, 1994.

own_words.text: Justices do not campaign or make policy promises. The official Voter Information Guide publishes a statement of qualifications only.
The SF Chronicle reports no disciplinary matters on the Commission on Judicial Performance database for any justice on the 2026 ballot.
